Perth paediatrician Chia Saw, who was arrested and charged with alleged sexual conduct towards children, was snared by police thanks to a “vigilante” paedophile hunter, a court has heard.

Saw, 41, was arrested and charged last month with multiple counts of indecent dealing and indecent recording of children - some of whom were allegedly patients of his. He was also charged with one count of sexual penetration of a child under 16.

On Friday Saw applied yet again to be released on bail while his charges proceed through the courts, but it was once again adjourned without a decision being made.

But as the magistrate weighed up his decision, more information surrounding the allegations against Saw were revealed.

Saw’s defence lawyer Alex Smith told Perth Magistrates Court that while police claimed he was engaging with a child while they were at school, he was, in fact, engaging with what he called, “a vigilante paedophile hunter” who was pretending to be a child.

That person, who is not a police officer or an employee of the police, allegedly engaged in multiple conversations with Saw under the guise they were a child. Those conversations were then allegedly handed to the police as potential evidence against him.

“This is a person who doesn’t exist,” Smith said.

“They established an account on some sort of social media app and engaged in conversations with the accused - presented himself as a child and engaged in this conversation.

“That third party gave those messages to police.”

But Smith did concede alleged communication Saw had with a separate child who had been a patient, was “unprofessional”. He also argued that Saw allegedly engaged with her because she was an “extremely troubled young person in the care of the Department [of Communities]. [Saw had] concern for her welfare and wanted to develop a rapport.”

One of the messages Saw sent a child said, “I saw you waiting out the school today ... have a nice weekend.”

While Saw’s application for bail has been delayed another week while a report is prepared to gauge his suitability for home detention with an ankle monitor, prosecutors said there were going to be five more charges coming, adding that there were possibly six or seven alleged complainants that still needed to be interviewed by police.

“It’s a complex, ongoing investigation,” they said.

The court heard Saw’s wife, a general practitioner, would move out of their family home with their two young daughters if he were to be granted bail.

“While these charges are serious and inherently draw abhorrence by the community at large, these are allegations at this point in time,” the magistrate said.

Saw will be back before the court on July 10 to hear the outcome of his bail application.
